item.title: Pre-market briefing — 2026-08-13
item.description:
THE SETUP

Futures are pointing to a firmly higher open, with the S&P set to build on last night's record close and the Nasdaq leading. The tape is digesting a genuinely mixed prior session — broad index strength alongside brutal single-stock reactions in two of the most-watched tech names — while the rates market continues to price a softening labor backdrop against a Fed that hasn't moved. Vol is quiet, the dollar is soft, and the curve has bull-steepened into today's session. Three things matter most: first, whether the post-CPI, post-payrolls repricing in front-end yields extends or stalls, since that's the engine behind the equity melt-up; second, Applied Materials reports after tonight's close, and given how violently the market reacted to Cisco's beat-and-guide overnight, positioning into AMAT is unusually fraught; third, crude's sharp overnight slide on demand-outlook cuts is a genuine cross-asset signal worth watching beyond the energy complex alone.

OVERNIGHT TAPE

S&P 500 futures are up sharply, with Nasdaq 100 futures outperforming and the Dow and Russell lagging — a continuation of the mega-cap-tech-led tone from the prior close. Asia was mixed: the Nikkei extended its advance as semiconductor and artificial intelligence-related shares followed Wall Street higher , while Hang Seng and Shanghai both slipped modestly. Europe closed lower across the board ahead of the US open, a quiet fade rather than anything catalyst-driven. Vol is notably subdued — VIX sits well below its 20-day average, with the futures curve still in contango, signaling no near-term hedging stress even with two major tech names getting hit hard overnight. The dollar index is soft, extending its recent drift lower, with yen and yuan both firming slightly against it while sterling is marginally weaker.

RATES AND THE FED

The curve richened across the belly and long end, with every tenor from 6-month out to 30-year posting a lower yield on the day while bills barely moved. The 2s10s spread remains solidly positive and the 3m10y spread is even wider, both consistent with a curve that has fully normalized out of inversion and continues to steepen as the market prices a Fed that's done hiking and increasingly likely to ease. The move is being driven by the same two data points reshaping the whole macro debate this week: a softer-than-expected labor market and CPI that cooled further. Fed commentary around the edges is leaning toward validating the market's dovish read — additional cuts are anticipated through the remainder of 2026 by a growing share of the sell-side, though that view is not universal and hinges on whether the growth slowdown implied by the jobs data is confirmed or reverses.

The one complication for the long end is fiscal, not monetary. Yesterday's 30-year bond auction cleared at the highest interest rate in a quarter of a century , a reminder that even as cyclical data argues for lower yields, term premium and supply concerns are working in the opposite direction at the long end — which is part of why the 30-year yield fell by less on the day than the belly of the curve. With effective fed funds unchanged and no FOMC meeting until after the minutes release next week, this remains a data- and supply-driven rates market rather than one waiting on a specific Fed decision.

MACRO

The data flow this week has been unambiguously soft on the labor side and cooler on inflation, and both are pulling in the same directional direction for policy even if the internals are messy. Nonfarm payrolls printed -23,000, a genuine contraction versus the prior month's +20,000, while the unemployment rate actually ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2% — leaving investors with mixed signals on whether this is labor-supply noise or a real demand-side crack. Initial claims at 209,000 versus a prior 200,000 add a little confirmation to the softening narrative without being alarming on their own. On the inflation side, CPI YoY eased to 3.3% from 3.5%, core CPI to 2.5% from 2.6%, and core PCE to 3.3% from 3.4% — a broad-based, if modest, cooling. Real GDP growth also slowed to 1.5% SAAR from 2.1%. Nothing on today's calendar is scheduled to test this narrative directly; the next real test is the FOMC minutes release next week, which the market will comb for confirmation of the dovish read now priced into the front end.

RANKED DEVELOPMENTS

record fourth-quarter 2026 results and strong AI-fueled guidance , yet the stock fell sharply after hours, even as investors digest the sharp rally and margin signals that had built into the print. This is a warning sign for positioning heading into Applied Materials tonight: strong fundamentals are not preventing air-pocket reactions when expectations and prior rallies have run ahead of the numbers. Read as neutral-to-cautionary for the AI-capex trade broadly — the fundamentals remain intact, but the market is now pricing perfection, and any incremental disappointment is being punished disproportionately. Watch AMAT's after-hours reaction tonight as the next data point.

a sector-wide selloff tied to China export-control overhang and cyclicality concerns in memory and foundry capex. This is bearish for semiconductor-equipment sentiment into the print and a read-through risk for the broader AI-capex complex if guidance disappoints tonight. Watch the after-hours reaction and any read-through to Micron, KLA, and Lam Research tomorrow.

OPEC also cut its demand forecast for 2026 and, separately, world oil demand is forecast to decline according to the IEA's latest report. This is a genuine growth-signal datapoint layered on top of the soft labor print — both are consistent with a slowing global demand backdrop, which is disinflationary and rate-cut-supportive but also a mild negative read on global growth. Bearish for energy-linked equities and breakevens, modestly supportive of the bond rally. Watch whether energy-sector price action decouples from the broader risk rally today.

gold pulls back from a two-month high as markets reassess the Fed rate outlook , alongside broader softness in silver. This looks like profit-taking after a strong run rather than a change in the medium-term thesis, but it's worth flagging as the metals complex has been one of the most crowded macro trades this year. Neutral-to-bearish near term for precious metals; watch real yields for the next directional cue.

MOVERS

Pre-market, Applied Materials is the standout decliner ahead of tonight's report, extending a slide that saw shares fall after hours despite the earnings beat framework playing out across the group; Micron is a bright spot, tracking the same AI-memory demand narrative that's been supportive of the group generally. Philip Morris is firmer in a defensive bid, while Abbott and Booking are both softer, though no specific catalyst stands out for either move — both look like continuation of prior-session drift rather than news-driven repricing.

In the prior session, Cisco was by far the most dramatic mover, falling on nearly triple average volume even after delivering record fourth-quarter 2026 results and strong AI-fueled guidance — a textbook sell-the-news reaction given how far the stock had run into the print. Arista and Applied Materials both fell alongside it as networking and equipment names de-rated together, while ConocoPhillips slipped with crude. On the gainer side, Intuit, Netflix, Palantir, Adobe, and Micron all posted strong single-day gains, with Intuit's move on above-average volume the most conviction-backed of the group; the others traded on lighter-than-average volume, suggesting more short-covering or momentum-chasing than fresh institutional conviction.

CATALYSTS, NEXT 1–2 WEEKS

The most consequential item on the calendar is the FOMC minutes from the July 28-29 meeting, due next Wednesday, which the market will parse for confirmation or pushback on the dovish repricing now embedded in the front end of the curve. Retail earnings cluster heavily next week — Home Depot, Target, Lowe's, TJX, and then Walmart the following Wednesday — and collectively they're the best read the market gets on consumer health heading into year-end, particularly relevant given the growth slowdown implied by recent GDP and labor data. Treasury supply remains heavy throughout, with bill auctions continuing alongside a 20-year bond auction next Wednesday and a 29-year bond auction the day after — worth watching given how much attention this week's 30-year sale drew on pricing. Further out, Nvidia's report on August 26th is the single largest event risk for the AI-capex thesis broadly, with Analog Devices, Deere, Salesforce, Synopsys, and Intuit's next quarter also on the docket that week.

item.title: Pre-market briefing — 2026-08-12
item.description:
I'll research the overnight narrative context before drafting the briefing.

Pre-Market Briefing — Wednesday, August 12, 2026

The Setup

Futures point to a firm open with the S&P and Nasdaq extending Tuesday's gains while the Dow lags, and volatility has collapsed overnight even as the single most important data point of the summer lands before the bell. The tape is broadly risk-on: growth and small-caps are bid, the VIX is sitting well below its 20-day average, and gold is spiking alongside — not instead of — a firmer dollar, an unusual combination worth watching rather than explaining away. Three things matter today, in order: first, the July CPI print at 8:30am ET, the swing factor for the rate-cut debate and the reason the curve has already rallied into the release; second, the AI-infrastructure earnings complex — Dell, Oracle, Arista, Micron, Super Micro — that is doing the heavy lifting for Nasdaq futures and setting up Applied Materials' print tomorrow as the next read-through; third, a cluster of consumer-discretionary and mega-cap communication-services names (Home Depot, Uber, Lululemon, Meta) that sold off hard in the prior session without a clean single catalyst, raising the question of whether this is rotation or noise.

Overnight Tape

Risk assets are firmer across the board pre-market. S&P futures are up +0.30% , Nasdaq 100 futures are leading at +0.80%, Russell 2000 futures are up +0.67%, while Dow futures are the outlier at -0.10% — a split that lines up with the sector story below: tech and small-cap strength against Dow-heavy softness. Asia was broadly strong: the Nikkei 225 ran +1.63%, helped mechanically by a weaker yen (dollar/yen +0.12%) that supports exporter earnings; Shanghai added +0.51%; the Hang Seng was roughly flat at -0.19%. Europe, which has already closed for the session, finished softer — Stoxx 600 -0.16%, DAX -0.23%, FTSE 100 -0.10% — a quiet fade rather than anything dramatic. The standout is volatility: the VIX is down -4.8% to 14.55, well under its 17.0 20-day average, with the curve in contango (VIX3M at 18.53). That's a notably calm vol posture heading into a high-importance CPI release — either genuine confidence in the disinflation trend, or complacency that gets tested at 8:30am. The dollar index is up +0.18% even as gold rallies +1.89% and silver +1.50%, a divergence that doesn't resolve into a single clean narrative and is worth flagging as such rather than forcing a story onto it.

Rates and the Fed

The Treasury curve rallied modestly into the CPI print, with yields lower across nearly every tenor and the front end leading: the 1-year fell -3 bps to 4.00%, 2-year and 3-year both fell -2 bps to 4.20% and 4.25%, and 10-year fell -2 bps to 4.68%. The move looks like positioning for a softer print or at least confirmation that disinflation is intact, though the magnitude is modest — this is a lean, not a conviction bet. The curve itself remains solidly positive: 2s10s at +48 bps and 3m10y at +81 bps, a long way from the inversions that defined prior cycles, and the shape has been reinforced by the deterioration in the labor data discussed below. The effective fed funds rate is steady at 3.63%, unchanged from the prior reading, and there's no FOMC meeting between now and the minutes from the July 28–29 meeting due August 19 at 2:00pm ET — those minutes are the next scheduled window into how divided the committee was on the cut path. Today's auction slate adds supply to watch alongside the data: a $42 billion 10-year note auction and a $72 billion 17-week bill auction both price today, with a $25 billion 30-year bond auction following tomorrow. A soft CPI print combined with weak demand at the 10-year auction would be a genuinely bullish rates combination; a hot CPI print into weak auction demand is the scenario that would hurt both bonds and equities simultaneously. The vol backdrop — cheap and in contango — suggests the market isn't currently pricing that tail heavily.

Macro

The backdrop into today's CPI print is unambiguously softer on growth and labor even as inflation has been cooling. The latest CPI reading stands at 3.3% year-over-year, down from a prior 3.5%, and core CPI is at 2.5%, down from 2.6% — both released today at 8:30am ET, comparing against those prior levels. Core PCE, the Fed's preferred gauge, was last at 3.3% versus a prior 3.4%, with the next reading due August 26. The labor picture is the more striking piece: nonfarm payrolls fell -23,000 against a prior +20,000, a genuine deterioration, even as the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2% — a combination that doesn't tell one clean story and likely reflects participation dynamics rather than labor-market strength. Initial jobless claims ticked up slightly to 199,000 from 198,000, with tomorrow's claims report the next incremental data point. Real GDP growth slowed to 1.5% QoQ SAAR from a prior 2.1%, reinforcing the deceleration theme. Collectively, this is a market pricing a Fed increasingly torn between still-present inflation and a visibly cooling economy — a dynamic one recent analysis characterized directly, noting the report has arrived at a critical juncture for financial markets given the mix of inflation and labor signals. Retail sales on August 14 is the next release that could meaningfully shift this narrative.

Ranked Developments

Movers

The overnight and prior-session mover list splits cleanly into a confirmed-catalyst AI/hardware complex and a consumer/mega-cap decline that lacks a single confirmed news driver. Cisco is the standout pre-market decliner at -4.1% to $118.84, but the company doesn't report earnings until after tonight's close — this move looks like de-risking or positioning ahead of the print rather than a reaction to confirmed news, and should be treated as such. The rest of the pre-market tape — Netflix +1.1%, Micron +1.0%, Deere +1.0%, Applied Materials +0.9% — is modest and consistent with a broad risk-on tone rather than idiosyncratic news, with Deere in particular not on today's earnings calendar (its print isn't until August 20). On the prior-session gainer side, Super Micro's +19.0% move on 3.3x average volume stands out as the cleanest signal of genuine news; Dell, Arista, and Oracle's moves also carry above-average or in-line volume consistent with earnings-driven repricing. On the loser side, Uber, Lululemon, Meta, Home Depot, and GM all fell 2.9%–4.0%, but several came on below-average volume — Meta at 0.9x, Home Depot at 0.8x, GM at just 0.5x — which argues against a single confirmed catalyst for each name individually; the more defensible explanation is the sector rotation visible in the data (consumer discretionary and communication services were the two weakest sectors), and any name-specific driver beyond that should be treated as unconfirmed.

Catalysts, Next 1–2 Weeks

The next two weeks are front-loaded with the events most likely to move rates and equities together. Today's CPI print is the most immediate repricing risk, followed closely by retail sales on August 14, which will speak directly to whether the consumer-discretionary weakness seen in the prior session is fundamental or technical. The FOMC minutes on August 19 are the next real window into the Fed's internal debate, and the run of retail earnings that week — Home Depot, Target, TJX, Lowe's, Walmart — will stress-test the consumer read from multiple angles simultaneously. Further out, Nvidia's report on August 26, alongside GDP and Personal Income/Core PCE the same day, is the single biggest event risk left in the month given Nvidia's weight in the AI-capex narrative that's currently driving sector leadership.
